item.title: Claude Models and Model Selection
item.description:
Simple definition#

Anthropic sells Claude in tiers. Bigger tiers reason better and cost more; smaller tiers are faster and cheaper. Inside each model you also choose an effort level — how hard the model thinks before it answers. Model selection for Claude is therefore a two-dimensional choice: which tier and how much effort, made per task and checked against your own evaluation set.

item.title: The Claude API for Builders
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Claude API is one HTTP endpoint, POST /v1/messages: you send a model ID, optional system instructions, a list of messages and optional tools; Claude returns content blocks (text, tool calls, thinking). Everything else — tools, structured output, caching, citations, files — is a feature of that one endpoint or a small supporting API (Batches, Files, Models, Token counting). Official SDKs exist for Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C# and PHP.

item.title: Claude Code in Practice
item.description:
Simple definition#

Claude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding tool. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands and integrates with your development tools — in the terminal, VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, a desktop app, the browser (cloud sessions), mobile, Slack and CI. It is a harness around a Claude model: the model reasons and decides; Claude Code supplies the tools, manages what goes into the context window, and enforces permissions.

item.title: Claude Code Best Practices Cheatsheet
item.description:
Simple definition#

Claude Code’s defaults already do the right thing for most prompts: auto mode, Opus 5.5 at medium effort, automatic sub-agents and automatic compaction. Best practice is mostly about the few things no default can know — what is not in your repo, how to check the work, which rules can never bend, and what you are willing to spend.

item.title: Claude Code Commands Cheatsheet
item.description:
Simple definition#

You drive Claude Code three ways: slash commands inside a session (/compact, /rewind), CLI subcommands and flags from your shell (claude -p, claude mcp add), and keyboard shortcuts (Esc, Shift+Tab). Some slash commands are bundled skills (/code-review, /loop, /batch) — prompts Claude follows rather than fixed built-ins. Type / in a session to see everything available, including your own skills and plugin commands.

item.title: Claude Code Hooks Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

A hook is your own handler — a shell command, an HTTP endpoint, an MCP tool, or a model prompt — that Claude Code runs at a fixed point in its loop, such as before a tool call or when Claude tries to finish. Unlike CLAUDE.md, a command or HTTP hook is deterministic: the harness runs it every time, whatever the model decided. Hooks are how you make a rule hold with zero exceptions.

item.title: Claude Code Settings Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

Claude Code reads JSON settings files at several levels — your user file, the project’s shared and local files, and the organisation’s managed settings — and combines them into one effective configuration. Settings control what Claude may do (permissions, sandbox), which model it uses, what loads into context, which extensions run, and what is reported. Environment variables cover authentication, providers and a few low-level limits.

item.title: Claude Code Skills Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: YAML frontmatter saying what it is and when to use it, followed by Markdown instructions. Claude sees every skill’s description in each session and loads the body only when the skill is invoked — by you typing /skill-name, or by Claude deciding it fits the task. Skills hold procedures and team knowledge that would otherwise bloat CLAUDE.md.

item.title: Claude Code Sub-agents Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

A sub-agent is a separate Claude worker that the main conversation hands a task to. It has its own context window, its own system prompt, and optionally its own tools, model and permission mode. It does the work and returns a summary, so long searches, test logs or file dumps never enter your main conversation. Claude delegates on its own when a sub-agent’s description fits; you can also ask for one by name.

item.title: Claude Code MCP Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Claude Code is an MCP client: each MCP server you add — a local process or a remote URL — contributes tools (and optionally resources and prompts) that Claude can call, such as “query the database”, “read the Jira ticket” or “fetch the Sentry error”. For the protocol itself, see Model Context Protocol.

item.title: Claude Code Plugins Reference
item.description:
Simple definition#

A plugin is a directory that bundles Claude Code extensions — skills, sub-agents, hooks, MCP servers, language servers, output styles and more — so they install, update and enable as one unit. A marketplace is a catalogue (usually a Git repository with a marketplace.json) that lists plugins and where to fetch them. Plugins are how a team or organisation shares one Claude Code setup across many repositories and machines.

item.title: Claude Code Output Styles and Status Line
item.description:
Simple definition#

An output style changes how Claude talks to you for a whole session — its role, tone, length and format — by adding instructions to every request. The status line changes what you see while it works: a bar under the prompt rendered by your own script from live session data (model, context use, cost, git branch, rate limits). Neither changes what Claude is allowed to do.

item.title: Claude Agent SDK
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library. From Python or TypeScript you call query(), and the SDK runs the same agent loop, built-in tools (read, edit, shell, search, web), permissions, sessions, hooks, sub-agents and MCP support that power the Claude Code CLI — inside a process you operate. You supply the prompt, the tools it may use, and callbacks that decide what it’s allowed to do.

item.title: Claude Code Automation and Parallel Work
item.description:
Simple definition#

Once Claude Code can check its own work, it no longer needs you at the keyboard. Automation means starting runs from a script, a timer or an event (claude -p, GitHub Actions, /schedule). Parallel work means running several Claude workers at once — sub-agents inside a session, background sessions in agent view, coordinated agent teams, or a scripted dynamic workflow — usually each in its own git worktree.

item.title: Claude Code for Teams and Organisations
item.description:
Simple definition#

For a team, Claude Code configuration has three owners. The repository carries shared conventions, permissions, hooks, skills, agents and MCP servers, committed like any other code. Each developer keeps personal preferences in local and user files. The organisation sets policy through managed settings that no one else can override, and watches usage and spend through analytics and telemetry.

item.title: Claude Code Troubleshooting
item.description:
Simple definition#

Most Claude Code problems are one of three things: something didn’t load (a file in the wrong place, a typo, an unapproved server), something else overrode it (a higher-precedence setting, a managed policy), or the environment is in the way (PATH, network, proxy, terminal). Look at what actually loaded before guessing, isolate with safe mode, and change one thing at a time.

item.title: Claude Across the SDLC
item.description:
Simple definition#

Using Claude across the software development lifecycle (SDLC) means giving it a defined job in each phase — not just autocomplete while coding. In every phase the pattern is the same: context in (the artefacts that phase needs), a specific task, a verification step, and a human decision where accountability sits.

item.title: Using Claude Intelligently
item.description:
Simple definition#

Using Claude intelligently means getting reliable, verified results at the lowest sensible cost and risk. It rests on five habits: give the right context, ask for a clear outcome, make the result verifiable, pick the right model and effort, and keep a human accountable for what ships.
